column9: What does an enzyme do?
column14: Speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up
column15: Speeds up a chemical reaction but is used up as it works
column16: Slows chemical reactions down so cells can control them
column17: Becomes part of the new product the reaction makes
column28: An enzyme speeds up a chemical reaction and comes out unchanged, ready to be used again. It isn't used up, it speeds reactions up instead of slowing them down, and it doesn't become part of the products; the substrate is what gets changed into products.
column29: Think of the enzymes in your saliva working on a cracker. Do they make digestion faster or slower, and are they still there afterward?

column9: Enzymes belong to which group of macromolecules?
column14: Carbohydrates
column15: Lipids
column16: Proteins
column17: Nucleic acids
column28: Enzymes are proteins: folded chains of amino acids. Their folded shape forms the active site, which is why heat and the wrong pH (both of which change a protein's shape) can stop them.
column29: A sample of pure enzyme would turn Biuret solution purple.

column9: The enzyme that breaks down the sugar **maltose** follows the usual enzyme naming rule. Its name is ___.
column28: Enzyme names usually end in -ase and often start with the substrate's name: maltose → maltase, lactose → lactase, sucrose → sucrase. Maltase breaks maltose into two glucose molecules.
column29: Lactase breaks down lactose. Change the ending the same way.

column9: Based on its name, which of these is most likely an enzyme?
column14: Cellulose
column15: Glycogen
column16: Galactose
column17: Cellulase
column28: Cellulase ends in -ase, the usual enzyme ending; it breaks down cellulose. Humans don't make cellulase, which is why we can't digest fiber. Cellulose and galactose end in -ose like most sugars, and glycogen is a polysaccharide.
column29: Many sugars end in -ose. What ending do most enzyme names share?

column9: Chemists add a ___ to a reaction to make it go faster, and they get it back unchanged at the end. Enzymes are the kind made by living things.
column28: Catalyst is the general name for anything that makes a reaction go faster and comes out unchanged, like the platinum in a car's exhaust system. Enzymes are the catalysts made by living things, which is why they are called biological catalysts; that phrase means enzymes, not every catalyst.
column29: Platinum in a car's exhaust system is one too. The word starts with c.

column9: Match each part of the lock-and-key model to its description.
column14: Enzyme :: The molecule that speeds up the reaction
column15: Substrate :: The molecule the enzyme acts on (the key)
column16: Active site :: The pocket on the enzyme where the substrate fits (the lock)
column17: Products :: The new molecules released when the reaction is done
column28: The enzyme is the molecule that speeds up the reaction. The substrate is the key it acts on. The active site is the lock, the pocket shaped to fit only that substrate. The products are released at the end, and the enzyme is free to work again.
column29: The key fits into the lock, and when the lock turns, something new comes out.

column9: When too much heat or the wrong pH makes an enzyme unfold and lose its 3-D shape, the enzyme has been ___.
column28: A denatured enzyme has lost its 3-D shape, so its active site no longer fits the substrate and it stops working. Denaturing is usually permanent.
column29: Cooking an egg does this to the proteins in egg white, and it usually can't be undone.

column9: One enzyme can speed up almost any reaction in the body, as long as the temperature is right.
column28: False. Enzymes are specific: each active site fits only one substrate (or a few very similar ones). Lipase breaks down fats, but it won't touch proteins or starch.
column29: Think of a lock and key. Does one key open every lock in the school?

column9: An enzyme's **optimum** temperature is the temperature at which the enzyme —
column14: has its highest activity
column15: first begins to work at all
column16: is destroyed and stops working
column17: stops moving and freezes solid
column28: The optimum is the best temperature: where activity is highest. Below it the enzyme works more slowly; far above it the enzyme denatures and stops.
column29: Optimum means best.

column9: Most enzymes in the human body work best at about 37 °C, which is normal body temperature.
column28: True. Human enzymes have an optimum near body temperature, about 37 °C. That's one reason your body works hard to keep its temperature steady.
column29: Normal body temperature is 98.6 °F. What is that in °C?

column9: Amylase in your saliva works in your mouth. At about what pH does it work best?
column14: About 2
column15: About 7
column16: About 10
column17: About 13
column28: Amylase in saliva works best near pH 7 (neutral), the pH of your mouth. pH 2 is stomach acid. Very basic values like 10 or 13 would change amylase's shape.
column29: Your mouth is not acidic like your stomach, and it's not basic like bleach.

column9: Amylase in your saliva starts breaking down which macromolecule in a cracker?
column14: Protein
column15: Fat
column16: DNA
column17: Starch
column28: Amylase breaks starch (a polysaccharide) into smaller sugars. That's why a cracker starts to taste a little sweet if you chew it long enough. Proteins and fats are broken down by other enzymes.
column29: Crackers are made mostly of flour. What kind of complex carbohydrate is in flour?

column9: Match each enzyme to the substrate it breaks down.
column14: Lactase :: Lactose (milk sugar)
column15: Sucrase :: Sucrose (table sugar)
column16: Lipase :: Lipids (fats and oils)
column17: Protease :: Proteins
column28: Enzymes are usually named for their substrate plus -ase: lactase → lactose, sucrase → sucrose, lipase → lipids, protease → proteins.
column29: Most enzyme names start with the name of their substrate.

column9: How do enzymes speed up chemical reactions?
column14: They lower the activation energy of the reaction
column15: They add extra heat energy to the reaction
column16: They raise the activation energy of the reaction
column17: They become part of the products of the reaction
column28: Activation energy is the energy needed to get a reaction started. Enzymes lower it, so the reaction can run quickly at body temperature. They don't add heat, they don't raise the hill, and they come out unchanged instead of becoming part of the products.
column29: Think of a reaction as a hill that has to be climbed before it can go. Do enzymes make the hill bigger or smaller?

column9: People who are lactose intolerant don't make enough lactase, so the lactose in milk isn't broken down well.
column28: True. Without enough lactase, lactose (milk sugar) isn't broken down in the small intestine, which causes the stomach trouble of lactose intolerance. Lactose-free milk and lactase pills are ways around it.
column29: Lactase is the enzyme for lactose. What happens to a reaction when its enzyme is missing?

column9: Lactase breaks down lactose but has no effect on sucrose, even though both are disaccharides. What is the best explanation?
column14: Sucrose is a protein, so lactase can't work on it
column15: Sucrose's shape doesn't fit lactase's active site
column16: Lactase gets used up after breaking down lactose
column17: Sucrose was already denatured by stomach acid
column28: Enzymes are specific. Lactase's active site is shaped to fit lactose, so sucrose, a differently shaped disaccharide, doesn't fit. Sucrose is a carbohydrate, not a protein; enzymes aren't used up; and denaturing means a large folded molecule like an enzyme losing its shape, so it doesn't describe a small sugar like sucrose.
column29: Think of a lock and key. What has to match for a key to work?

column9: What is the **enzyme-substrate complex**?
column14: The new product molecules that are released when the reaction is finished
column15: An enzyme that has lost its 3-D shape because it was heated too much
column16: The substrate held in the active site while its bonds are broken or built
column17: Two enzymes that have stuck together to form one larger protein
column28: The enzyme-substrate complex is the moment the substrate is held in the active site and the reaction happens. The released molecules are the products, a heat-damaged enzyme is denatured, and two joined enzymes don't include a substrate.
column29: The name tells you which two things are joined together at that moment.

column9: Put the steps of an enzyme reaction in order, from first to last.
column14: The products are released from the active site
column15: The substrate fits into the enzyme's active site
column16: The enzyme is free to bind a new substrate
column17: Bonds in the substrate are broken or built while the enzyme holds it
column28: First the substrate binds in the active site. Then the enzyme breaks or builds its bonds. The products are released, and the unchanged enzyme can bind another substrate.
column29: The key goes into the lock, the lock turns, the door opens, and the key is ready to use again.

column9: Data table for catalase in potato: Temperature (°C): 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55 | Foam height (mm): 6, 14, 22, 30, 19, 4. At what temperature did catalase work best?
column28: The tallest foam (30 mm) is at 35 °C, so that's the optimum in this data. Activity rises from 5 to 35 °C and falls after that as catalase starts to denature.
column29: More foam means more enzyme activity. Find the tallest foam, then read its temperature.

column9: Data table for an enzyme: Temperature (°C): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 | Reaction rate: 4, 12, 22, 34, 15, 2, 0. Which statement best describes the data?
column14: The rate rises steadily the whole time, so a hotter enzyme is always faster
column15: The rate is highest at 0 °C, because cold protects the enzyme's shape
column16: The rate stays about the same no matter what the temperature is
column17: The rate rises to a peak at 30 °C, then drops quickly as the enzyme denatures
column28: The rate climbs from 4 to 34 as molecules move faster, peaks at 30 °C (the optimum), then falls to 15, 2, and 0 as heat unfolds the enzyme. It doesn't keep rising, it's near its lowest at 0 °C, and it clearly changes.
column29: Read the rates from left to right. Where do they stop going up?

column9: Pepsin breaks down proteins and works best at pH 2. Kai mixes pepsin and egg-white protein in a beaker at pH 8 and 37 °C. Very little protein is broken down. Why?
column14: The higher pH changes pepsin's shape, so proteins can't fit its active site
column15: Pepsin only works inside the body, so it can't work in a beaker
column16: The pepsin was used up before the protein was added
column17: At 37 °C the beaker was too hot, so the pepsin denatured
column28: pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum of 2, so its shape (and its active site) changes and the egg-white protein can't bind. Enzymes can work outside the body when conditions are right, enzymes aren't used up, and 37 °C is body temperature, near the optimum for human enzymes, not hot enough to denature them.
column29: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. What happens to an enzyme's shape far from it?

column9: Data table for an enzyme: pH: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 | Bubbles per minute: 2, 9, 24, 40, 11. What is this enzyme's optimum pH?
column14: pH 5
column15: pH 7
column16: pH 9
column17: pH 11
column28: The most bubbles (40 per minute) are at pH 9, so that is the optimum. Activity drops on both sides: at pH 11 the enzyme is losing its shape, and at pH 3 it barely works.
column29: Find the most bubbles in the table, then read the pH that goes with it.

column9: In the potato lab, catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). What is the foam made of?
column14: Hydrogen gas
column15: Oxygen gas
column16: Carbon dioxide gas
column17: Water vapor
column28: Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas: 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. The bubbles in the foam are oxygen, so more foam means more enzyme activity. No hydrogen gas or carbon dioxide is made.
column29: H₂O₂ breaks into two products. One is a liquid you drink; the other is a gas you breathe.

column9: Hannah's group tests potato pieces at 5, 25, 45, and 65 °C and measures how tall the foam gets. What is the **dependent variable**?
column14: The temperature of the potato
column15: The amount of hydrogen peroxide
column16: The height of the foam
column17: The size of each potato piece
column28: Foam height is what the group measures, and it depends on the temperature, so it is the dependent variable. Temperature is the independent variable (what they change). The amount of hydrogen peroxide and the size of each piece should be kept the same (constants).
column29: The dependent variable is the effect: the thing you measure to see what happened.

column9: Tyler drops one whole potato cube into hydrogen peroxide. Rosa dices an identical cube into tiny pieces and drops them into the same amount of hydrogen peroxide. Who gets more foam, and why?
column14: Tyler, because a whole cube holds more catalase than the small pieces
column15: Rosa, because dicing warms the potato up to its optimum temperature
column16: Neither, because both of them used the same amount of potato
column17: Rosa, because dicing lets more of the potato's catalase touch the peroxide
column28: Dicing creates more surface area, so more catalase meets the substrate at once and more foam forms. Both cubes hold the same total amount of enzyme, and dicing doesn't change the temperature. How much enzyme touches the substrate, not just how much potato there is, controls how fast the reaction goes.
column29: Both used the same amount of potato. Which one lets more of it touch the liquid?

column9: Which statements about enzymes are true? Select all that apply.
column14: They raise the activation energy of a reaction
column15: Each enzyme fits only certain substrates
column16: Each enzyme has an optimum pH where it works best
column17: They work only outside of living cells
column18: They speed up reactions by adding extra heat
column19: They can be denatured by high heat
column28: Enzymes are specific (lock and key), each has an optimum pH and temperature, and high heat can denature them. They lower activation energy instead of raising it or adding heat, and most of them work inside living cells.
column29: Check each statement on its own. Picture the lock-and-key model and an enzyme activity graph, and keep only the statements both pictures agree with.

column9: Why can a very high fever (above about 41 °C) be dangerous?
column14: Some of the body's enzymes can start to denature and stop working
column15: The extra heat makes every enzyme work too fast for the body to control
column16: Heat makes the body build far too many new enzymes at once
column17: Enzymes melt and turn into fats when the body gets too hot
column28: Human enzymes work best near 37 °C. At very high temperatures their shape starts to change, so the active site no longer fits and important reactions slow or stop. Enzymes don't speed up out of control past the optimum, and they are proteins, not fats.
column29: 41 °C is well above the best temperature for human enzymes. What happens to an enzyme's shape when it gets too hot?

column9: Food lasts longer in the refrigerator because the cold denatures the enzymes in the food and in bacteria.
column28: False. Cold slows enzymes down because molecules move more slowly, but it doesn't denature them. That's why food still spoils, just slowly, in the fridge. Heat and the wrong pH are what denature enzymes.
column29: Does cold destroy an enzyme's shape, or does it just slow the enzyme down?

column9: Lipase breaks fats down into which smaller molecules?
column14: Many amino acids
column15: Glycerol and fatty acids
column16: Glucose and fructose
column17: Sugars and phosphates
column28: A fat (triglyceride) is one glycerol plus three fatty acids, so lipase breaks it back into glycerol and fatty acids by hydrolysis. Amino acids come from proteins, glucose and fructose from a carbohydrate (sucrose), and sugars and phosphates from nucleic acids.
column29: Go back to the monomers. What two building blocks make up a fat molecule?

column9: Lactase breaks lactose (milk sugar) into which two monosaccharides?
column14: Glucose and fructose
column15: Glucose and glucose
column16: Glucose and galactose
column17: Fructose and galactose
column28: Lactose = glucose + galactose, so lactase splits it into those two. Glucose + fructose is sucrose, and glucose + glucose is maltose.
column29: Recall the three disaccharides: sucrose, maltose, and lactose. Which pair of sugars goes with milk sugar?

column9: Match each enzyme to where it works in the body.
column14: Salivary amylase :: Mouth
column15: Pepsin :: Stomach
column16: Trypsin :: Small intestine
column17: Catalase :: Liver and nearly every cell
column28: Salivary amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth. Pepsin digests protein in the acidic stomach (pH 2). Trypsin continues protein digestion in the small intestine (pH 8). Catalase works in the liver and almost every cell, breaking down toxic hydrogen peroxide.
column29: Follow your food: mouth, then stomach, then small intestine. One enzyme is everywhere because it cleans up a toxic chemical.

column9: If you add more enzyme while there is still plenty of substrate, the reaction will usually go faster.
column28: True. More enzyme means more active sites working at the same time, so more substrate is changed each second. This only helps while there is extra substrate waiting.
column29: More enzyme means more active sites. What happens when more locks are open for the keys?

column9: Why do living things need enzymes?
column14: Without them, cells would have no way to get the carbon atoms they need
column15: Enzymes are the main way the body stores extra energy for later
column16: Enzymes are needed so reactions can happen at much higher temperatures
column17: Without them, most reactions in cells would happen far too slowly
column28: Most reactions in cells would still happen without enzymes, but far too slowly. Enzymes let them run fast at body temperature (starch in seconds instead of years). Enzymes aren't a carbon source or stored energy, and they let reactions run at low temperatures, not high ones.
column29: Starch could break down on its own, but it would take years. What would that mean for a cell that needs energy right now?

column9: Raising the temperature of an enzyme from 10 °C to 30 °C usually slows it down, because any heat damages enzymes.
column28: False. Below the optimum, warming speeds an enzyme up because molecules move faster and substrates bump into active sites more often. Only temperatures well past the optimum damage (denature) an enzyme.
column29: Picture the left side of an enzyme temperature graph, before the peak. Which way does the line go?

column9: Group 3 measured foam heights of 24 mm, 30 mm, and 27 mm in three trials at 35 °C. What is their average foam height? Answer in mm.
column28: Average = (24 + 30 + 27) ÷ 3 = 81 ÷ 3 = 27 mm. Running several trials and averaging them makes the data more reliable.
column29: Add the three trials, then divide by the number of trials.

column9: An energy table for one reaction. **Without the enzyme:** starts at 20 kJ, peaks at 80 kJ, ends at 5 kJ. **With the enzyme:** starts at 20 kJ, peaks at 45 kJ, ends at 5 kJ. What is the activation energy of the reaction **with** the enzyme? Answer in kJ.
column28: Activation energy is the climb from where the reaction starts up to the peak: 45 − 20 = 25 kJ with the enzyme (80 − 20 = 60 kJ without it). The peak itself (45 kJ) is not the activation energy, and the ending energy (5 kJ) doesn't matter for the climb. The enzyme lowers the hill; the start and end stay the same.
column29: Activation energy is the hill the reaction has to climb to get going. Where does the climb start, and where is the top?

column9: Kayla keeps one potato piece in the freezer overnight and boils another for 5 minutes. She lets both return to room temperature, then adds hydrogen peroxide to each. What will she most likely see?
column14: The frozen piece foams, but the boiled piece makes little or no foam
column15: The boiled piece foams, but the frozen piece makes little or no foam
column16: Neither piece foams, because both enzymes were denatured
column17: Both pieces foam the same, since both are back at room temperature
column28: Cold slows catalase but doesn't denature it, so once the frozen piece warms up the enzyme works again. Boiling denatures catalase, and that change is usually permanent, so warming it back up doesn't help. That's why a boiled potato makes almost no foam.
column29: Which treatment only slowed the enzyme down, and which one changed the enzyme's shape for good?

column9: Ben puts identical potato pieces into 5 mL of hydrogen peroxide at different strengths and measures the foam after 30 seconds. Data table: H₂O₂ concentration (%): 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 | Foam height after 30 s (mm): 10, 20, 28, 30, 30. Why does the foam stop increasing after 2%?
column14: The catalase in each potato piece is used up after making 30 mm of foam
column15: Every active site is already busy, so more substrate can't speed it up
column16: The stronger hydrogen peroxide denatured the potato's catalase
column17: The potato pieces ran out of starch for the catalase to break down
column28: With a fixed amount of enzyme, raising the substrate concentration helps only until every active site is working. After that, extra H₂O₂ molecules have to wait their turn, so the foam made in 30 seconds levels off at 30 mm. Enzymes aren't used up; if the peroxide had denatured the catalase, the foam would drop instead of holding steady; and starch isn't catalase's substrate (hydrogen peroxide is).
column29: Every potato piece is the same, so every trial has the same amount of enzyme. What limit does the stronger peroxide run into?

column9: Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down proteins. Gelatin (Jell-O) is made of protein. Fresh pineapple keeps Jell-O from setting, but canned pineapple, which is heated during canning, does not. Why?
column14: Canning heat sped the enzyme up until it was all used up
column15: The sugary syrup in the can fills up the enzyme's active site
column16: Heat during canning denatured the pineapple's enzyme
column17: Canning heat widened the active site so more gelatin fits in it
column28: Canning heats the pineapple enough to denature its protein-digesting enzyme, so it can no longer break down the gelatin and the Jell-O sets. Enzymes aren't used up by the reactions they speed up. Sugar from the syrup doesn't fit the active site of a protein-digesting enzyme, because enzymes are specific. And an active site that fit more gelatin would break down more of it, so the Jell-O still wouldn't set.
column29: What does high heat do to any protein, including an enzyme?

column9: Which of these would most likely slow down or stop the catalase in a potato? Select all that apply.
column14: Dicing the potato into small pieces
column15: Boiling the potato first
column16: Adding more hydrogen peroxide
column17: Soaking the potato in vinegar (an acid) first
column18: Testing it at room temperature instead of in ice water
column19: Soaking the potato in a strong base first
column28: Boiling denatures catalase, and soaking in an acid like vinegar (about pH 3) or a strong base moves it far from its optimum pH, which changes its shape. Dicing adds surface area, more H₂O₂ adds substrate, and room temperature is warmer than ice water, so those keep or increase the foam.
column29: Which choices would change the enzyme's shape? Which ones would actually help it?

column9: Data table: pH: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 | Enzyme A activity: 35, 90, 55, 15, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0 | Enzyme B activity: 0, 0, 0, 5, 20, 45, 75, 95, 60. Which conclusions are supported by the data? Select all that apply.
column14: Enzyme A works best at pH 2
column15: Enzyme B would work well in the stomach
column16: At pH 5, both enzymes are far below their highest activity
column17: Enzyme B works best in a slightly basic environment
column18: Both enzymes stop working completely at pH 7
column28: Enzyme A peaks at pH 2 (90), like pepsin in the stomach. Enzyme B peaks at pH 8 (95), slightly basic, like trypsin in the small intestine. At pH 5, A is at 5 and B is at 20, both far below their peaks. B is at 0 in very acidic conditions, so it would not work in the stomach, and B is still at 75 at pH 7.
column29: For each enzyme, find its highest number first. Then check each statement against the table.

column9: Aiden says, "Enzymes work faster when they're warmer, so heating the potato to 90 °C will give the most foam." Which response is best?
column14: He's right: enzyme activity keeps rising for as long as the temperature rises
column15: He's wrong: catalase works best near freezing, so warming slows it down
column16: He's right: boiling uses up the hydrogen peroxide faster, which makes more foam
column17: He's wrong: far above the optimum, catalase denatures and stops working
column28: Warming does speed catalase up, but only to its optimum. Far above it the enzyme unfolds (denatures), which is why a boiled potato makes almost no foam. Catalase works better at room temperature than near freezing, and the drop in foam isn't caused by the peroxide being used up.
column29: He's half right. Warming helps up to a point. What happens after that point?

column9: A poison molecule gets stuck in an enzyme's active site and won't come out. What happens to that enzyme's reaction?
column14: It slows or stops, because the substrate can't get into the active site
column15: It speeds up, because the poison gives the reaction extra energy
column16: Nothing changes, because a substrate can bind anywhere on an enzyme's surface
column17: The enzyme breaks the poison down and turns it into new substrate
column28: The substrate has to fit into the active site to react. With the active site blocked, the substrate can't bind, so the reaction slows or stops. Substrates don't bind just anywhere on an enzyme, and the poison doesn't add energy or become substrate.
column29: If someone jams a broken key into a lock, can the right key still get in?

column9: **Sucralose** is a sweetener made from table sugar (sucrose) by swapping three small parts of the molecule for chlorine atoms. It tastes sweet, but your body gets almost no energy from it. Which explanation is best?
column14: It denatures your digestive enzymes as soon as it reaches your stomach
column15: Its changed shape doesn't fit the active site of a digestive enzyme
column16: It is broken down so quickly that its energy escapes as body heat
column17: It is a protein, so your body uses it for building instead of energy
column28: Swapping in chlorine atoms changes the molecule's shape. Sucralose still tastes sweet, but it doesn't fit the active site of the enzyme that splits sucrose, so it isn't broken down into glucose and fructose and passes through your body mostly unchanged. It doesn't denature your enzymes (you still digest the rest of your meal), its energy doesn't escape as heat, and it is made from a sugar, not a protein (proteins can give the body energy anyway).
column29: Enzymes are picky about shape. What if a molecule only looks like a sugar to your taste buds?

column9: Marcus is lactose intolerant. A lactase pill contains the enzyme lactase. Which plan makes the most sense for Marcus, and why?
column14: Take it once his stomach starts to hurt, which shows lactose is there
column15: Take it with each meal, so the lactase can also break down starch in bread
column16: Take it with his first bite of dairy, so the lactase meets the lactose
column17: Take one pill a week, since enzymes aren't used up and can be reused
column28: Lactase has to meet lactose to work, so the pill goes in with the first bite of dairy. By the time his stomach hurts, the undigested lactose has already moved on to the large intestine, where gut bacteria feed on it and make gas, so it's too late. Lactase is specific: it breaks down lactose, not the starch in bread. And enzymes aren't used up by the reactions they speed up, but the pill's lactase gets digested and moves through the gut like other food, so one pill won't last a week.
column29: An enzyme has to meet its substrate to work. When is the lactose in his digestive system?

column9: Hydrogen peroxide foams when it's poured on a fresh cut, but not much on unbroken skin. What is the best explanation?
column14: Warm blood heats the peroxide enough for it to break down on its own
column15: Unbroken skin is too cool for the peroxide to break down quickly
column16: The foam is blood proteins being denatured as the peroxide soaks into the cut
column17: Damaged cells in the cut release catalase, which breaks down the peroxide
column28: Catalase is inside your cells. In a cut, damaged cells and blood release catalase, so it meets the hydrogen peroxide and breaks it down quickly, making foam. On unbroken skin, the tough outer layer keeps the peroxide away from most living cells. The foam is a gas made by the reaction, not denatured protein. Temperature isn't the difference either: skin and blood are both warm, and without catalase the peroxide breaks down far too slowly to foam.
column29: Catalase is inside nearly every living cell. What happens to cells in a cut?

column9: A potato cube is tested for catalase activity as it is slowly heated from 20 °C to 95 °C. Put what happens to the enzyme in order.
column14: Catalase is fully denatured and makes almost no foam
column15: Catalase reaches its optimum and makes the most foam
column16: Catalase speeds up as molecules move faster
column17: Catalase begins to lose its shape and the foam starts to drop
column28: As it warms, catalase speeds up (molecules move faster and collide more), reaches its optimum (most foam), starts to denature (foam drops), and finally is fully denatured (almost no foam). The denaturing is usually permanent.
column29: What does warming do to how fast molecules move? And what happens to an enzyme's shape once it gets too hot?

column9: In the potato lab, rate of reaction = average amount of foam ÷ reaction time. A group measured 16 mL, 20 mL, and 18 mL of foam in three trials, each lasting 4 minutes. What was the rate of reaction? Answer in mL/min.
column28: Average foam = (16 + 20 + 18) ÷ 3 = 54 ÷ 3 = 18 mL. Rate = 18 mL ÷ 4 min = 4.5 mL/min. Dividing the total (54 mL) by the time skips the averaging step, and dividing by the 3 trials gives the average foam, not the rate.
column29: Average the three trials first, then divide by the time.

column9: Lena's group ran one trial at each temperature. Data table: Temperature (°C): 35, 45, 55, 65, 75 | Foam height (mm): 28, 24, 41, 9, 2. Lena says this proves 55 °C is catalase's optimum. Which response is best?
column14: One odd trial isn't proof; run more trials at each temperature and average
column15: She's right: whichever trial made the tallest foam marks the optimum
column16: The 2 mm result at 75 °C is the real mistake, so they should redo that trial
column17: Change the 41 to a number that fits the pattern, then finish the graph
column28: The foam falls from 35 to 45 °C and keeps falling after 55 °C, so the single 41 mm trial breaks the pattern and may be a mistake (a bigger potato piece or extra peroxide). Repeating trials and averaging makes the data reliable. One odd number isn't proof of an optimum, the tiny 2 mm at 75 °C fits the pattern of a denatured enzyme, and changing data is never okay.
